book_context: Final coda after the treaty is burned and Mr. Brown (Sir James) is unmasked at the Savoy supper. The book has run a joint venture of Tommy and Tuppence that began with Tuppence scorning sentiment and planning to marry money. It also ran Julius's photograph-born infatuation with Jane, his businesslike proposal to Tuppence (which she declined because she loves Tommy), and Tommy's jealous outburst when he believed her dead. The chapter mirrors two couples in two cars both detouring via Regent's Park. It closes the 'adventure/sport' motif that opened in the Lyons' tea shop.
continuity_checks: Julius and Jane ride in the Rolls-Royce; Tommy and Tuppence ride in a taxi; both go via Regent's Park to the Ritz.
'Head over ears' is said first by Julius about Beresford, then echoed by Tuppence about Julius.
Carter offered the Government job and Julius the American ranch post. Do not swap them.
Tommy's uncle line (if kept) presupposes the Savoy chapter's Sir William reconciliation.
Tuppence, not Tommy, says 'Ours'. Tommy speaks the last line.

essential: Julius and Jane are driving back to the Ritz in the Rolls-Royce. He praises her toast and her courage. She says she feels tired, lonesome and homesick.

Julius proposes and mentions the Embassy invitation as the alternative. He has loved her since seeing her photo. He promises patience and to 'set you free' if she never loves him. He wants the right to look after her.
Keep Julius's hustling comedy: the special license 'to-morrow morning' right after promising not to hustle her.
Jane accepts with a declaration of present love, tied to the bullet grazing his cheek.

The Regent's Park detour joke: Jane asks if it is a long way from the Savoy to the Ritz, and Julius replies 'It depends how you go.' Julius admits he held the supper at the Savoy to get her alone, away from Tuppence. He confirms Beresford is 'head over ears'. Jane deduces this from what Tuppence didn't say.
Tommy and Tuppence sit stiff and tongue-tied in a taxi on the same route. Their old camaraderie has gone.
Tommy forbids Tuppence to marry Julius. She says Julius asked only out of kindness and loves Jane. Keep the 'sterling worth' tease and Tommy's flustered reply.
Futures: Tommy will 'stick to the old ship', meaning Carter's job, rather than Julius's ranch post, because she'd be at home in London. Keep 'I don't see where I come in' / 'I do'.
Money: Tuppence knows the size of their cheques but won't tell. This reprises her mercenary trait.
Tuppence's furnishing reverie leads to 'Ours'. Tommy embraces her and says he owes her for squashing his sentiment.
Tuppence remarks that this hasn't really been a proposal, though it beats Julius's 'rotten' one. Tommy says she won't get out of marrying him.
End on marriage as 'a sport', keeping her list of conventional names for marriage briefly and Tommy's closing line.
optional: Paragraph 16-17: the chauffeur's wages joke can be cut, but keep Julius's Savoy confession and the Siamese-twins line in condensed form.
Paragraphs 26-28 and 31-32: the beats of strained silence can collapse into one sentence.
Paragraphs 41-43: Tommy's condescending remarks on Jane can be trimmed to one line.
Paragraph 46: 'I like your uncle, Tommy' can be cut, but keep it framed as a diversion leading into the job question.
Paragraphs 54-56: the cheque exchange can be compressed to a single tease.
Paragraph 59: the furnishing list can be shortened to two or three items, but must still lead into 'flat' and 'Ours'.
Paragraph 68: the list of marriage descriptors can be shortened, but keep its contrast with 'A sport'.
risks: The 600-word target is tight given the dialogue-driven comedy. Favour compressing narration over cutting the punchlines.

voice_profile: Brisk, comic third-person narration, mostly carried by quick dialogue. Christie's lightness depends on understatement and ironic narrative asides ('with a singular lack of originality'), speech tags that colour delivery (dictatorially, meekly, demurely, condescendingly, unblushingly), and clipped exchanges ending on a punchline. Julius speaks American slang (sure thing, hustle, I guess). Tommy is gruff and laconic. Tuppence is pert, mercenary and teasing, and covers feeling with banter. Sentiment is shown obliquely, through silence, evasion and jokes, never stated straight.
